strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and clearly articulated idea: replacing iterative densification in 3DGS with a one-step dense initialization built from triangulated dense 2D correspondences, which shortens the optimization path and places Gaussians near surfaces from the start.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation on three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) against a wide range of baselines spanning both quality-focused (Mip-Splatting, 3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS, AbsGS) and speed-focused (Taming-3DGS, gsplat, EAGLES, MiniSplatting, 3DGS-LM) methods, with training times measured on consistent hardware and initialization cost included for their method.

Consistently strong results: at 30K steps the method beats quality-focused baselines on SSIM and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians (~60% of 3DGS), and at 5K steps it is competitive with efficiency-focused baselines, demonstrating genuine Pareto improvements in time/quality/splat-count.

Thorough ablation studies: comparison of matching backbones (RoMa, LoFTR, DKM, RAFT), depth-based initialization alternative, effect of densification on different initializations, noise robustness analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity (reference views, keypoints per view), and an insightful analysis of Gaussian motion/path length showing the reduced parameter-space travel.
Demonstrated composability: combining the initialization with Taming-3DGS yields further gains, supporting the claim that the method is orthogonal to optimization-side accelerations.
Includes honest discussion of failure modes (reflective/view-dependent surfaces) and qualitative evidence for improved high-frequency detail recovery.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism (triangulating dense 2D matches via DLT least squares, Eq. 4-7) is textbook multiple-view geometry, and the contribution is largely pipeline integration of a strong pretrained matcher (RoMa) with 3DGS. The paper itself notes prior work using random or SfM initialization; the delta over such ideas is more empirical than conceptual.

Heavy dependence on a large pretrained dense matching network raises questions about generality (domains where RoMa fails, e.g., textureless, reflective, or non-Lambertian scenes) and about the fair attribution of cost, since matcher inference is a substantial one-time expense compared to sparse SfM keypoints.

PSNR gains are weak or absent: on Mip-NeRF360, Ours+3DGS (27.80) is below Mip-Splatting (27.97) and 3DGS-MCMC (28.15); the claims of superiority rest mainly on SSIM/LPIPS. The narrative that the method 'outperforms quality-focused state-of-the-art' is somewhat overstated relative to Table 1.

Internal inconsistencies in claims: the abstract states 'only half the splats' and '25% of the training time,' while the conclusion states '40% fewer Gaussians' and 'six times fewer optimization steps'; these should be reconciled.

No variance reporting, statistical significance testing, or repeated runs; comparisons to published numbers on different GPUs (A6000/RTX3090 vs. A100) introduce uncertainty in the time-based claims, even though the authors rerun key baselines.

The densification-free setting is shown to slightly underperform densified variants on some poorly covered regions (Tab. 2, supp. Fig. A6), meaning 'eliminating densification' is not strictly optimal; the paper could better characterize when densification should be retained.

Some presentation issues: the theoretical framing (Sec. 3.3) is verbose for what is standard triangulation, and several cross-references/claims (e.g., 'ptimisation' typo, inconsistent splat-count numbers) suggest the manuscript would benefit from careful polishing.

strengths: The core idea is clean, well-motivated, and clearly presented: replace incremental densification with a one-shot dense initialization obtained by triangulating dense 2D correspondences (RoMa), giving every Gaussian an informed position, color, and scale from the start. This is a fundamentally different angle from most 3DGS acceleration work, which modifies the optimizer, rasterizer, or densification criterion.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly fair: three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), comparisons against speed-optimized (Taming-3DGS, gsplat, EAGLES, MiniSplatting, 3DGS-LM), quality-focused (3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS, Mip-Splatting, AbsGS), and initialization-based baselines (RAIN-GS), with initialization cost explicitly included in the reported runtimes — a common fairness pitfall that the authors avoid.

Results are convincing: Ours+3DGS 30K and Ours+Taming 30K achieve best or second-best LPIPS/SSIM on most benchmarks while using ~40-60% fewer Gaussians, and Ours+Taming reaches comparable perceptual quality in ~25-40% of the training time of competing methods (Table 1, Fig. 1).

Thorough ablation studies: matching-network choice (RoMa/LoFTR/DKM/RAFT, Table 3), initialization type including depth-based alternatives (Table 2), sensitivity to initialization noise (Fig. 6), hyperparameters such as number of reference views and matches per view (Fig. 7), and a novel analysis of Gaussian travel distance and path length in parameter space (Fig. 5) that directly supports the paper's central hypothesis.
Demonstrated composability with an orthogonal acceleration method (Taming-3DGS) and useful extras such as extreme-viewpoint robustness (Fig. 4) and per-scene results in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on an external, large-scale pretrained model (RoMa). A substantial fraction of the method's benefit likely derives from the quality of RoMa's dense correspondences rather than the triangulation/initialization pipeline itself, which is essentially classical multi-view triangulation. The paper's ablations (Table 3) confirm that performance tracks matcher quality, which both limits novelty and raises generalization concerns on domains where RoMa underperforms.

The headline claim of 'eliminating densification' is overstated. Table 2 shows the authors' own method still improves slightly with densification (PSNR 27.84 vs 27.80, LPIPS 0.173 vs 0.175), so densification is a design choice rather than a true redundancy; the paper would be more accurate to frame this as reduced reliance on densification.

The efficiency claims are selectively supported: at 5K steps the method's PSNR clearly trails baselines (e.g., 26.70 vs 27.49 for 3DGS* on Mip-NeRF360; 22.95 vs 23.57 for gsplat on T&T), and the 'matching them in evaluation metrics' claim (Sec. 4.3) holds mainly for LPIPS/SSIM, not PSNR.

Scalability and practical cost of the initialization are underexplored. The method requires dense matching over ~180 reference images plus up to 15,000 keypoints per frame; behavior on large-scale scenes, memory/compute scaling with image count, and failure modes in textureless or reflective regions (acknowledged in Sec. 4.3) are only briefly discussed.

Moderate novelty: dense-matching-based point cloud generation followed by Gaussian optimization is a natural combination adjacent to existing directions (e.g., RAIN-GS, InstantSplat, Radsplat); the contribution is a careful, well-executed instantiation and analysis rather than a new technical mechanism.

Presentation issues that should be corrected: several typos ('ptimisation', 'absoulte'), Eq. (6) presents b as a zero vector in a homogeneous least-squares system without clarifying the scale-fixing convention, and per-scene PSNR of exactly '32' for two indoor scenes in Table A2 suggests rounding/sloppiness.

strengths: The core idea is clean, well-motivated, and clearly articulated: replacing iterative densification with a one-shot dense initialization obtained by triangulating dense 2D correspondences (RoMa) between image pairs. This is a conceptually simple change to the 3DGS pipeline that yields a disproportionate improvement, and the paper convincingly argues why (shorter optimization path, per-pixel supervision from the start).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) against a broad set of baselines spanning quality-focused (3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS, Mip-Splatting, AbsGS) and efficiency-focused (Taming-3DGS, 3DGS-LM, gsplat, EAGLES, MiniSplatting) methods. Training times for competitors were re-measured on the same hardware, and the one-time correspondence-computation cost is reportedly included in the reported times, which is a fairness point many papers neglect.

Strong headline results: the 5K-step variants are competitive with or better than efficiency methods at comparable times, and the 30K variants achieve best/second-best LPIPS and SSIM on most metrics (e.g., LPIPS 0.174/0.121/0.210 vs. 3DGS's 0.215/0.169/0.242) while using fewer Gaussians than 3DGS in the default configuration.

Thorough ablation studies: comparison of matching networks (RoMa/LoFTR/DKM/RAFT, depth-based initialization), quantified Gaussian motion analysis (Eqs. 9-10, Fig. 5) supporting the 'shorter parameter-space path' claim, noise robustness analysis (Fig. 6), hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 7), effect of re-enabling densification (Tab. 2), and per-scene results in the supplementary.

Demonstrated compatibility/orthogonality: initializing Taming-3DGS with the proposed method gives further gains (e.g., Tanks&Temples PSNR 24.93 vs. 24.34), supporting the claim that the method is a pluggable initialization improvement rather than a competing pipeline.

Generally good reproducibility signals: implementation built on the original 3DGS codebase, hardware specified, densification disabled with gradient aggregation removed, supplementary implementation details, and a notation table.
weaknesses: Inconsistencies and overstatements in the headline claims. The conclusion states EDGS exceeds 'quality-focused' approaches, but in Tab. 1 the 30K PSNR on Mip-NeRF360 (27.80 / 28.06) is below 3DGS-MCMC (28.15) and Mip-Splatting (27.97); the advantage is real for LPIPS/SSIM but not uniformly for PSNR, and the paper should qualify this. Similarly, the abstract says '60% of splats' and '25% of training time' while the conclusion says 'six times fewer optimization steps and approximately 40% fewer Gaussians,' and the introduction says 'half the splats' — the numbers vary across the paper and need tightening.

Dependence on a heavyweight pretrained dense matcher (RoMa) raises practical concerns that are underexplored. The cost of computing dense correspondences for many image pairs (15000 keypoints/reference, 180 reference views) is folded into training time, but the paper does not break out how much of the reported time is matching/triangulation versus optimization, nor how the method scales to very large image collections. RoMa's own training data/bias may also limit generalization to domains unlike the benchmarks, which is not tested (only three capture-centric datasets).

The triangulation formulation uses only pairwise (two-view) matches with least squares (Eqs. 4-8); multi-view redundancy, occlusion handling, and filtering of inconsistent matches are only implicitly addressed through confidence aggregation. Error analysis of the triangulated points (e.g., reprojection error statistics, fraction of outliers surviving) is not reported, even though the paper argues the initialization is the key driver.

Fairness caveats in comparisons are handled unevenly: some baseline numbers are taken from papers run on different GPUs (A6000/3090, marked with symbols), and for 3DGS-LM the Gaussian counts are assumed. The mixed provenance weakens the precision of the runtime and #G comparisons in Tab. 1.

The per-scene results reveal weaknesses not discussed: e.g., Ours+3DGS 30K SSIM on treehill is 0.655 and flowers 0.642, and the Taming-combined variant uses substantially more Gaussians on several scenes (6M on bicycle vs. 2.3M for Ours+3DGS), which partially undercuts the 'fewer splats' narrative for the best-performing configuration.

No variance reporting (seeds/repeated runs) for the main comparisons, and the ablation on densification (Tab. 2) shows densification still helps the proposed method slightly (27.84 vs 27.80), leaving open questions about when eliminating densification is genuinely optimal rather than merely more efficient.
Presentation issues: typos ('ptimisation', 'absoulte'), a somewhat verbose narrative introduction, and Fig. 5 axis descriptions that are hard to parse; these are correctable but reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea is clear, well-motivated, and technically sound: replacing iterative densification with a one-shot dense initialization from triangulated dense correspondences (RoMa), together with a geometry/confidence-based sampling distribution and SH coefficient estimation, is an elegant reframing of the 3DGS optimization path.

Comprehensive evaluation on the three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) with retrained baselines on identical hardware. Results are strong: best or second-best SSIM/LPIPS with fewer Gaussians and comparable training time (Tab. 1), and LPIPS improvements are substantial (0.141 vs 0.176 for 3DGS-MCMC on Mip-NeRF360).

The paper goes beyond headline numbers: Gaussian trajectory analysis (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4) directly supports the claimed mechanism of shorter optimization paths, and the ablations (Tab. 6, Fig. 6, Fig. 7) are thorough, covering sampling distribution components, SH initialization, matching algorithms, hyperparameter sensitivity, and robustness to initialization noise.

Compatibility experiments (Tab. 3) showing EDGS works as a plug-and-play initialization for AbsGS, 3DGS-MCMC, and Taming 3DGS increase the practical value of the contribution, and the comparison against alternative initializations (DepthFM, VGGT, denser COLMAP in Tab. 7 and Tab. A2) convincingly rules out the trivial explanation that any dense/better prior suffices.

The supplementary material is extensive and supports reproducibility: implementation details, timing breakdowns (~120 s initialization), thresholds, memory footprint, per-scene results, and a notation table.
weaknesses: Dependence on a pretrained dense matcher (RoMa) is a material limitation. RoMa was trained largely on scanned scenes, and the paper does not probe generalization to imagery that is out-of-distribution for RoMa (e.g., reflective/textureless/deformable content, non-Lambertian materials), where dense matching and hence triangulation quality may degrade. The method still fundamentally requires COLMAP-calibrated poses, so the SfM dependency is shifted rather than removed.

The contribution is somewhat engineering-flavored: triangulation of correspondences is classic multi-view geometry, and the novelty lies mainly in the sampling distribution design and its use as a densification replacement rather than in new technical machinery. Related work acknowledges RAIN-GS and 3DGS-MCMC show random init can match 3DGS; the paper should more sharply delineate what about the matched init (vs. coverage alone) drives the LPIPS gains, though Tab. A2 partially addresses this.

Quality gains are concentrated in perceptual metrics. On Mip-NeRF360, 3DGS-MCMC still achieves higher PSNR (28.15 vs 28.02), and the abstract/framing emphasizes '35% lower LPIPS' claims that should be tempered; PSNR improvements over strong baselines are modest and not uniformly across scenes (per-scene results in Tabs. A4-A6 show mixed PSNR).

Fairness of speed comparisons: EDGS training time includes initialization, which is commendable, but the method needs a large A100 GPU (up to 15 GB) for the initialization phase and its wall-clock advantage at full convergence is modest (23 m vs 19-20 m for several baselines in Tab. 1). The '8x faster' narrative in Fig. 1 applies to reaching baseline 3DGS quality, not to outperforming the strongest baselines.

Some claims are under-supported: the extreme-viewpoint analysis (Fig. 8) is qualitative on a single scene; the sparse-view experiment (Tab. A1) is on 7 scenes with selective exclusions (flowers, treehill) and shows mixed results versus SparseGS, so it should be framed as auxiliary rather than a strength.

Minor presentation issues: Tab. 7 header says 'Qualitative comparison' but reports quantitative metrics; Eq. (6)/(7) formulation with A^T and a zero vector b is awkwardly presented (the homogeneous solution is the null space, better described via SVD); scale initialization is only described in the supplement.

strengths: The core idea — replacing iterative densification with a one-shot dense initialization from triangulated dense correspondences — is well-motivated and clearly articulated, with the paper asking the pointed question of whether densification can be bypassed entirely.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), retrained baselines on identical hardware (Table 1), early-stopping comparisons against efficiency methods at matched budgets (Table 2), plug-in experiments showing EDGS improves AbsGS, 3DGS-MCMC, and Taming 3DGS as an initializer (Table 3), and per-scene results in the supplement.

Ablations are convincing and address the most obvious counter-explanations: the denser-COLMAP baseline (Table A2) shows the gains are not merely from more Gaussians, the initialization comparison (Table 7) covers random, COLMAP, monocular depth (DepthFM), and VGGT, and Table 6 decomposes the confidence and reprojection sampling terms plus SH initialization.

The analysis of Gaussian trajectories (Fig. 4, Eqs. 14–15), noise robustness (Fig. 7), and hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 6) provides genuine insight into *why* the method works, rather than only reporting aggregate metrics.

The method requires no modification to the optimization algorithm, making it directly compatible with existing 3DGS acceleration and densification techniques — a practical, transferable contribution. Implementation details (runtime breakdown, memory, thresholds) in Sec. A support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: triangulating matched pixels is classical multi-view geometry, and the contribution is essentially a well-engineered initialization pipeline built on a strong off-the-shelf matcher (RoMa). Much of the empirical gain plausibly stems from RoMa's quality rather than the pipeline itself, though Table 5 does show robustness across LoFTR/DKM/RAFT.

Heavy dependence on dense correspondence quality limits generalization: performance on scenes with repeated textures, reflective surfaces, dynamic content, or significant occlusion (where matchers fail) is not evaluated; all benchmarks are static, well-textured capture-style datasets.

Claims of surpassing state-of-the-art quality are somewhat overstated: on Mip-NeRF360 PSNR, 3DGS-MCMC (28.15) remains higher than EDGS (28.02), and on Deep Blending SSIM/PSNR, ScaffoldGS leads (0.907/30.25 vs. 0.904/29.81). EDGS leads mainly in LPIPS and under matched training-time comparisons.

Runtime comparisons, while honest about including initialization, should be scrutinized: initialization consumes ~120 s and 15 GB GPU memory of the ~27 m budget, so the favorable time comparisons partly depend on the reported initialization being relatively cheap versus its downstream savings; scalability to larger scenes with more reference views is not demonstrated.

PSNR improvements on indoor datasets are modest (e.g., 29.81 vs. 29.77 for retrained 3DGS on Deep Blending), meaning much of the headline gain is concentrated in LPIPS; the paper would be stronger with a direct geometric evaluation (e.g., depth accuracy) rather than only photometric metrics.

The paper cites the arXiv preprints it builds comparisons on (e.g., VGGT-X, 3DGS-LM) without noting their publication status or any limitations of reproduced rather than original results, and some baselines are noted as retrained with changed scene subsets (Scaffold-GS, 3DGS-MCMC on 7 of 9 scenes originally), introducing comparability caveats the text handles only briefly.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing iterative densification with a one-step dense initialization from triangulated dense correspondences, directly shortening the optimization path. The Gaussian motion analysis (Fig. 4, displacement and trajectory-length distributions) provides direct evidence for the claimed mechanism rather than only end metrics.

Comprehensive and mostly fair empirical evaluation: three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), competing methods re-evaluated on the same hardware, and EDGS runtimes explicitly include the ~120s initialization cost (Sec. A), which strengthens the speed claims.

State-of-the-art or near-SOTA results without densification: best SSIM/LPIPS on Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360 at comparable or fewer Gaussians (Tab. 1), and strong early-stopping results (Tab. 2) showing it matches or beats efficiency-focused methods at 5K/10K steps.

Thorough ablations covering the components that matter: matching algorithm choice (Tab. 5), the two sampling-distribution terms and SH initialization (Tab. 6), hyperparameter saturation (Fig. 6), and robustness to coordinate/color noise (Fig. 7).

The control experiment in Sec. E (denser COLMAP, 10x/50x duplication with noise) directly rules out the trivial 'more Gaussians' explanation, and Tab. 3 shows EDGS acts as a plug-and-play initializer that consistently improves ADC methods without increasing Gaussian count or training time.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed implementation settings (thresholds, number of reference views/neighbors/correspondences, timing breakdown, memory), a notation table, per-scene results, and sparse-view/robustness extensions in the supplementary.
weaknesses: Dependence on a pretrained dense matcher (RoMa) introduces an external learned prior whose failure modes are not fully characterized. The RAFT result in Tab. 5 shows the pipeline is sensitive to the matcher's design assumptions; behavior on textureless, reflective, transparent, or dynamic scenes where dense matching degrades is untested.

Conceptual novelty is moderate: triangulating correspondences to obtain 3D points is classical multiview geometry, and initialization-based improvements to 3DGS have been explored (e.g., RadSplat, VGGT-based init in Tab. 7). The contribution is best viewed as a well-executed systems/empirical advance rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Gains on PSNR are less consistent than on perceptual metrics (e.g., Mip-NeRF360 PSNR 28.02 vs 28.15 for 3DGS-MCMC), so headline claims rest mainly on SSIM/LPIPS; this is defensible but should be stated more carefully.

The method presumes accurate COLMAP camera poses and is evaluated only with posed inputs; the claim of broad applicability to realistic pipelines would benefit from discussion of pose-noise sensitivity, which is not studied.

Presentation inconsistencies: projection matrices are declared R^{4x3} in Sec. 3.3 but R^{3x4} in Tab. A9; Table 7 is labeled 'Qualitative comparison' though it reports quantitative metrics; several typos ('results or an NVIDIA RTX 3090'). These do not affect validity but should be corrected.

Some evaluation choices could invite scrutiny: results taken directly from papers for some baselines (Rain-GS), different hardware for some entries, and the ADC-integration experiment uses a different initialization size (140 views, 8.5k matches) than the headline configuration, though the authors document and justify this.
